The Lesser blind mole-rat (Nannospalax leucodon) exhibits a resting metabolic rate of 148.7 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 148.7 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value that aligns closely with the energetic demands of a subterranean lifestyle. This basal oxygen consumption reflects the substantial costs associated with burrowing through dense soils, which imposes considerable physiological constraints on the species. Comparative studies with other fossorial rodents indicate that this metabolic rate is moderate for an animal of its body size, suggesting adaptations that balance energy conservation with the mechanical work of excavation. The measurement was obtained from respirometry trials conducted on individuals that had been acclimated to laboratory conditions, ensuring that the readings represent a true resting state rather than activity-induced elevations. Such metabolic data are critical for understanding how this species manages its energy budget within the low-productivity environments it typically inhabits, where food resources such as geophytes and underground plant storage organs are patchily distributed.

Newborn pups of Nannospalax leucodon weigh approximately 6.25 grams [Wwb = approximately 6.25 grams] at parturition, a neonatal mass that is typical for altricial subterranean rodents of this lineage. This modest initial body mass places the neonates in a vulnerable state, entirely dependent on maternal care during the early postnatal period. Within the controlled thermal environment of the nest, maintained at around 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], females achieve a maximum reproductive rate of 2 to 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 4 pups per litter], produced across approximately 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters per year]. This reproductive strategy reflects the constraints of a subterranean existence, where litter sizes are relatively small to ensure that each offspring receives adequate nutritional investment from the mother. The frequency of litters is tightly linked to the seasonal availability of geophytes, which provide the energetic basis for lactation and post-partum recovery. Field observations further confirm that the interval between successive litters is regulated by the time required for pups to reach nutritional independence.

Adult females of this species attain an ultimate wet weight of 300 grams [Wwi = 300 grams], though considerable intraspecific variation exists, with individuals ranging from 162 to 504 grams depending on local habitat quality and seasonal food abundance. This body mass represents a substantial energetic investment for a fossorial mammal, and it is achieved through a prolonged period of somatic growth that extends well beyond the weaning stage. The maximum lifespan recorded for Nannospalax leucodon is approximately 7,373 days [am = approximately 7,373 days], a longevity estimate based on data from the closely related Nannospalax ehrenbergi at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Such an extended lifespan is remarkable for a rodent of this size and likely reflects the protective benefits of a subterranean habitat, which reduces exposure to aerial predators and extreme temperature fluctuations. Comparative analyses with other mole-rat species suggest that this longevity is associated with low extrinsic mortality rates in the underground environment, allowing individuals to survive for many years and reproduce across multiple seasons.

Gestation in the Lesser blind mole-rat lasts approximately 30 days [tg = approximately 30 days] when the mother maintains a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that is consistent with the relatively slow developmental pace observed in many fossorial mammals. Following birth, the pups remain in the natal nest and are completely dependent on maternal milk for sustenance. The weaning period, which marks the transition to independent feeding on solid food, occurs at 35 days after birth [tx = 35 days after birth], a benchmark that has been extrapolated from developmental patterns documented in Nannospalax ehrenbergi under thermoneutral conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. At this stage, the young begin to consume the same geophytes and underground roots that constitute the adult diet, signaling a critical shift in their nutritional ecology. The prolonged lactation period relative to many surface-dwelling rodents underscores the adaptive value of extended maternal investment in a habitat where juvenile foraging success hinges on the gradual acquisition of digging and navigation skills.

Sexual maturation in Nannospalax leucodon is a relatively delayed process, with puberty attained at 200 days after birth [tp = 200 days after birth] under thermoregulatory conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This protracted developmental timeline allows juveniles to achieve the body size and physiological competence necessary for the demanding tasks of burrow construction and territory defense. Upon reaching sexual maturity, individuals typically disperse from their natal tunnels to establish their own subterranean systems, a process that carries significant mortality risk. The reproductive schedule is further constrained by the energetic costs of pregnancy and lactation, which require a sustained high body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] to support foetal development and milk synthesis. Given the limited aboveground activity of this species, most ecological interactions—including mate location and resource competition—occur entirely within the underground tunnel network, shaping a life history that is finely tuned to the stable but resource-poor environment it occupies across its range in southeastern Europe.
